messages.subject: equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?
parts:
To avoid very long condition = ... && ... && ...

is there something equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?

If there isn't could someone help me get started on how to set this up? My js knowledge is, as yet, very limited.

messages.author: a814dd0eade31e3e
messages.subject: Re: equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?
parts:
I thought about how to do this for quite some time before posting ... and then a few minutes after posting I thought of a simple work around. Makes you wonder how (if) your brain works :)

interdepChoices <- c("hclustering","kmeansClustering")
notInAnd <- paste("input.tool != '",interdepChoices,"'", sep = "", collapse = " && ")

conditionalPanel(condition = notInAnd,
...
)

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?
parts:
Cool. To answer your original question though, this is how you might do it in JavaScript:

condition="['foo', 'bar', 'baz'].indexOf(input.tool) < 0"

Note that this shows the panel if input.tool is NOT one of foo, bar, baz; if you wanted it to show the panel if input.tool IS one of foo, bar, baz, just make the condition >= 0.

messages.subject: Re: equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?
parts:
To answer your original question in javascript, underscore contains will do the job:

!_.contains(["foo","bar","baz"], myThing);
-Alex

On Thursday, January 3, 2013 11:20:13 AM UTC-8, Alex Brown wrote:
I have had a lot of pleasure from underscore.js (Thanks Joe).  Not only does it attempt to solve some of the problems you want to solve, it is also it a good way to get clues on how ordinary javascript works.  

For example, map is an underscore function which iterates across a data structure, either an array or an object (there is not builtin map for objects)

In a browser debug console you can type the function name and see the internals.  

> _.map
function (e, t, n) {var r=[];return p&&e.map===p?e.map(t,n):(N(e,function(e,i,s){r[r.length]=t.call(n,e,i,s)}),r);}

This is the minified version of underscore, hence the crummy short names.  Let's visit the development version to see it in 'human':

  _.map = _.collect = function(obj, iterator, context) {
    var results = [];
    if (obj == null) return results;
    if (nativeMap && obj.map === nativeMap) return obj.map(iterator, context);
    each(obj, function(value, index, list) {
      results[results.length] = iterator.call(context, value, index, list);
    });
    return results;
  };

I wanted to see how object iteration worked, and it's delegated to 'each' which is also an underscore function

_.each= ...
   for (var key in obj) {
        if (_.has(obj, key)) {
          if (iterator.call(context, obj[key], key, obj) === breaker) return;
        }
      }
...

So it turns out it uses for (var key in obj) to iterate over an object; I've learned something new about javascript.

-Alex
